401:     localparam int unsigned NumBusySignals = 3;
402:     localparam int unsigned NumBusyBits = $bits(ibex_mubi_t) * NumBusySignals;
403:     logic [NumBusyBits-1:0] busy_bits_buf;
404:     prim_buf #(
405:       .Width(NumBusyBits)
406:     ) u_fetch_enable_buf (
407:       .in_i ({$bits(ibex_mubi_t){ctrl_busy, if_busy, lsu_busy}}),
408:       .out_o(busy_bits_buf)
409:     );
410: 
411:     // Set core_busy_o to IbexMuBiOn if even a single input is high.
412:     for (genvar i = 0; i < $bits(ibex_mubi_t); i++) begin : g_core_busy_bits
413:       if (IbexMuBiOn[i] == 1'b1) begin : g_pos
414:         assign core_busy_o[i] =  |busy_bits_buf[i*NumBusySignals +: NumBusySignals];
415:       end else begin : g_neg
416:         assign core_busy_o[i] = ~|busy_bits_buf[i*NumBusySignals +: NumBusySignals];
417:       end
418:     end
419:   end else begin : g_core_busy_non_secure
420:     // For non secure Ibex, synthesis is allowed to optimize core_busy_o.
421:     assign core_busy_o = (ctrl_busy || if_busy || lsu_busy) ? IbexMuBiOn : IbexMuBiOff;

998:       (outstanding_load_id  & load_store_unit_i.split_misaligned_access);

1001:       (outstanding_store_id & load_store_unit_i.split_misaligned_access);

1003:     // When writing back the result of a load, the load must have made it to writeback
1004:     `ASSERT(NoMemRFWriteWithoutPendingLoad, rf_we_lsu |-> outstanding_load_wb, clk_i, !rst_ni)

1018:   // Keep track of the PC last seen in the ID stage when fetch is disabled
1019:   logic [31:0]   pc_at_fetch_disable;
1020:   ibex_mubi_t    last_fetch_enable;
1021: 
1022:   always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
1023:     if (!rst_ni) begin
1024:       pc_at_fetch_disable <= '0;
1025:       last_fetch_enable   <= '0;
1026:     end else begin
1027:       last_fetch_enable <= fetch_enable_i;
1028: 
1029:       if ((fetch_enable_i != IbexMuBiOn) && (last_fetch_enable == IbexMuBiOn)) begin
1030:         pc_at_fetch_disable <= pc_id;
1031:       end
1032:     end

1035:   // A 1-bit encoding of fetch_enable_i to avoid polluting the NoExecWhenFetchEnableNotOn assertion

1042:   // ID/EX valid should not ressert once it has been cleared.
1043:   `ASSERT(NoExecWhenFetchEnableNotOn,
1044:           !fetch_enable_raw |=>
1045:           (~instr_valid_id || (pc_id == pc_at_fetch_disable)) && ~$rose(instr_valid_id))

10:   register_map_.push_back(
11:       std::make_unique<MSeccfgRegister>(kCSRMSeccfg, &register_map_));
12:   register_map_.push_back(
13:       std::make_unique<NonImpRegister>(kCSRMSeccfgh, &register_map_));
14:   // Instantiate all the registers
15:   for (unsigned int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
16:     uint32_t reg_addr = 0x3A0 + i;
17:     if (params->PMPEnable && (i < (params->PMPNumRegions / 4))) {
18:       register_map_.push_back(
19:           std::make_unique<PmpCfgRegister>(reg_addr, &register_map_));
20:     } else {
21:       register_map_.push_back(
22:           std::make_unique<NonImpRegister>(reg_addr, &register_map_));
23:     }
24:   }
25:   for (unsigned int i = 0; i < 16; i++) {
26:     uint32_t reg_addr = 0x3B0 + i;
27:     if (params->PMPEnable && (i < params->PMPNumRegions)) {
28:       register_map_.push_back(
29:           std::make_unique<PmpAddrRegister>(reg_addr, &register_map_));
30:     } else {
31:       register_map_.push_back(
32:           std::make_unique<NonImpRegister>(reg_addr, &register_map_));
33:     }
34:   }
35:   // mcountinhibit
36:   // - MSBs are always 0: unused counters cannot be inhibited
37:   // - Bit 1 is always 0: time cannot be disabled
38:   uint32_t mcountinhibit_mask =
39:       (~((0x1 << params->MHPMCounterNum) - 1) << 3) | 0x2;
40:   uint32_t mcountinhibit_resval = 0;
41:   register_map_.push_back(std::make_unique<WARLRegister>(
42:       0x320, &register_map_, mcountinhibit_mask, mcountinhibit_resval));
43:   // Performance counter setup
44:   for (unsigned int i = 3; i < 32; i++) {
45:     uint32_t reg_addr = 0x320 + i;
46:     if (i < (params->MHPMCounterNum + 3)) {
47:       register_map_.push_back(std::make_unique<WARLRegister>(
48:           reg_addr, &register_map_, 0xFFFFFFFF, 0x1 << (i - 3)));
49:     } else {
50:       register_map_.push_back(
51:           std::make_unique<NonImpRegister>(reg_addr, &register_map_));
52:     }
53:   }
54:   // mcycle
55:   register_map_.push_back(
56:       std::make_unique<BaseRegister>(0xB00, &register_map_));
57:   // minstret
58:   register_map_.push_back(
59:       std::make_unique<BaseRegister>(0xB02, &register_map_));
60:   // Generate masks from counter width parameter
61:   uint32_t mhpmcounter_mask_low, mhpmcounter_mask_high;
62:   if (params->MHPMCounterWidth >= 64) {
63:     mhpmcounter_mask_low = 0x0;
64:     mhpmcounter_mask_high = 0x0;
65:   } else {
66:     uint64_t mask = ~((0x1L << params->MHPMCounterWidth) - 1);
67:     mhpmcounter_mask_low = mask & 0xFFFFFFFF;
68:     mhpmcounter_mask_high = mask >> 32;
69:   }
70:   // Performance counter low word
71:   for (unsigned int i = 3; i < 32; i++) {
72:     uint32_t reg_addr = 0xB00 + i;
73:     if (i < (params->MHPMCounterNum + 3)) {
74:       register_map_.push_back(std::make_unique<WARLRegister>(
75:           reg_addr, &register_map_, mhpmcounter_mask_low, 0));
76:     } else {

79:     }

93:     } else {
94:       register_map_.push_back(

96:     }
97:   }
98: }

15: /**
16:  * Writes character to simulator out log. Signature matches c stdlib function

18:  *

20:  * @returns Character output (never fails so no EOF ever returned)
21:  */
22: int putchar(int c);
23: 
24: /**
25:  * Writes string to simulator out log.  Signature matches c stdlib function of

41:  * Immediately halts the simulation
42:  */

45: /**
46:  * Enables/disables performance counters.  This effects mcycle and minstret as
47:  * well as the mhpmcounterN counters.
48:  *
49:  * @param enable if non-zero enables, otherwise disables
50:  */
51: static inline void pcount_enable(int enable) {
52:   // Note cycle is disabled with everything else
53:   unsigned int inhibit_val = enable ? 0x0 : 0xFFFFFFFF;
54:   // CSR 0x320 was called `mucounteren` in the privileged spec v1.9.1, it was
55:   // then dropped in v1.10, and then re-added in v1.11 with the name
56:   // `mcountinhibit`. Unfortunately, the version of binutils we use only allows
57:   // the old name, and LLVM only supports the new name (though this is changed
58:   // on trunk to support both), so we use the numeric value here for maximum
59:   // compatibility.
60:   asm volatile("csrw  0x320, %0\n" : : "r"(inhibit_val));
61: }
62:

65:  * as the mhpmcounterN counters.

100:  * configurations that do not have an instruction cache and in particular is
101:  * safe to execute on those configurations.
102:  *
103:  * @param enable if non-zero enables, otherwise disables
104:  */
105: static inline void icache_enable(int enable) {
106:   if (enable) {
107:     // Set icache enable bit in CPUCTRLSTS
108:     asm volatile("csrs 0x7c0, 1");

1: // Copyright lowRISC contributors.

3: // SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
4: 
5: /*******************************************************************************
6:  * Directed test to check data independent timing feature
7:  *
8:  * This test uses a couple of functions, `count_ones_zeros` and `div_ones_zero`
9:  * that exhibit data dependent timing. This is via branch instructions in
10:  * `count_one_zeros` and via divide instructions in `div_ones_zeros`, which are
11:  * the only two types of instruction with data dependent timing in Ibex.
12:  *
13:  * The rest runs multiple iterations of each function providing input from an
14:  * LFSR, timing each iteration. The test passes where at least 25% of run times
15:  * differ for each function when data independent timing is disabled and where
16:  * all run times are identical for each function when data independent timing is
17:  * enabled.
18:  *
19:  * It does a second run with data independent timing enabled and the ICache
20:  * enabled. This time the functions must be called once with their timing result
21:  * discarded to warm up the ICache. With that done the function iterations must
22:  * exhibit identical timing as before for the test to pass.
23:  * ****************************************************************************/
24: 
25: #include "simple_system_common.h"
26: 
27: extern uint32_t count_ones_zeros(uint32_t n);
28: extern uint32_t div_ones_zeros(uint32_t n);
29: 
30: #define LFSR_POLY 0x80000057
31: #define NUM_ITERATIONS 100
32: #define INITIAL_VAL 0xDEADBEEF
33:

At each clock edge:
1. monitor_tick is called with the CURRENT values of csr_access_i, etc.
2. driver_tick provides new values for the NEXT cycle
3. NBA updates csr_access_i, etc.

But here's the key: monitor_tick is called BEFORE the NBA updates. So the monitor sees the values from the PREVIOUS NBA. And the driver_tick provides new values that will take effect via the CURRENT NBA.

But the monitor captures the outputs at the same clock edge as it captures the inputs. So if the inputs at clock edge N+1 indicate a READ of MINSTRET, the monitor would see the new value. This should match the C++ model.

OK, but the test is failing on a CLEAR operation, not a READ. For a CLEAR:

This means that a PREVIOUS write to MINSTRET that should have set it to 0x3108a91 didn't take effect. But I've verified that the write logic should work.

Let me try ONE MORE thing. Let me check if there's an issue with how Verilator handles the csr_op_e enum. Maybe the case statement for csr_op_i doesn't match correctly.

Actually, wait. Let me look at the monitor more carefully. The monitor passes csr_op_i as a 2-bit value. But in the C++ code:
```cpp
trans->csr_op = (CSRegisterOperation)op;
```

And the enum values are:
```cpp

  kCSRRead = 0,
  kCSRWrite = 1,
  kCSRSet = 2,
  kCSRClear = 3
};
```

But the DPI passes `const svBitVecVal *csr_op`, which is a 2-bit value. And the C++ code casts it to `CSRegisterOperation`. This should work.

But wait, what if the DPI function is not receiving the correct value? Let me check the DPI interface:
```systemverilog
reg_dpi::monitor_tick("reg_driver", rst_ni, illegal_csr_insn_o,
                      csr_access_i, csr_op_i, csr_op_en_i,
```


So csr_op is `bit [1:0]` (2 bits), and csr_op_i is of type `csr_op_e` (an enum with logic [1:0] base type). The conversion should be automatic.

And in my RTL:
```systemverilog

  CSR_OP_READ:  csr_wr = 1'b0;
```

steps.reasoning_content:
Now I can see the debug output. Let me trace through the MINSTRET transactions:

1. SET (op=2): wdata=0xe8a5dac0, rdata_before=0x00000000
   - After: minstret = 0 | 0xe8a5dac0 = 0xe8a5dac0
   
2. WRITE (op=1): wdata=0x5f2399cc, rdata_before=0x00000000
   - Wait, rdata_before=0? But after step 1, minstret should be 0xe8a5dac0!
   
3. WRITE (op=1): wdata=0x1bb28a95, rdata_before=0x5f2399cc
   - This shows the previous write took effect

4. CLEAR (op=3): wdata=0x00000000, rdata_before=0x1bb28a95
   - After: minstret = 0x1bb28a95 & ~0x00000000 = 0x1bb28a95 (unchanged)
   
5. CLEAR (op=3): wdata=0x00000000, rdata_before=0x00000000
   - Wait, rdata_before=0? After step 4, it should be 0x1bb28a95!

So the issue is that the register value is being LOST between transactions. After step 1, the register should be 0xe8a5dac0, but at step 2, rdata_before=0x00000000.

This suggests that the write from step 1 didn't take effect! But looking at the write logic, when csr_wr=1 and csr_addr_i=CSR_MINSTRET, minstret_lo_q should be updated.

Wait, let me look more carefully. Step 1 is a SET (op=2), not a WRITE. For a SET:
- csr_wdata_int = csr_rdata_o | csr_wdata_i = 0x00000000 | 0xe8a5dac0 = 0xe8a5dac0
- minstret_lo_q <= 0xe8a5dac0

But at step 2, rdata_before=0x00000000. This means the SET didn't take effect!

Why wouldn't the SET take effect? The write condition is `csr_wr && csr_addr_i == CSR_MINSTRET`. If csr_wr is true and csr_addr_i is CSR_MINSTRET, the write should happen.

Wait, but there's the mcycle increment issue! Looking at my minstret always_ff block:

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
  if (!rst_ni) begin
    minstret_lo_q <= '0;
    minstret_hi_q <= '0;
  end else begin
    if (csr_wr && csr_addr_i == CSR_MINSTRET)
      minstret_lo_q <= csr_wdata_int;
    else if (~mcountinhibit_q[2] & instr_ret_i)
      minstret_lo_q <= minstret_lo_q + 32'd1;
    if (csr_wr && csr_addr_i == CSR_MINSTRETH)
      minstret_hi_q <= csr_wdata_int;
  end
end
```

Wait, this should work. If csr_wr && csr_addr_i == CSR_MINSTRET, then minstret_lo_q = csr_wdata_int. Otherwise, if the counter should increment (which it doesn't since instr_ret_i = 0), it would increment.

But the debug shows that the SET didn't take effect. The rdata_before at step 2 is 0x00000000, meaning the SET at step 1 didn't update the register.

OH WAIT! I just noticed something crucial. Step 1 is a SET (op=2), and step 2 is a WRITE (op=1). But the rdata_before at step 2 is 0, not the expected 0xe8a5dac0 from the SET.

This means the SET at step 1 didn't write the value. But why?

Let me check: for a SET, csr_wdata_int = csr_rdata_o | csr_wdata_i. And csr_wr should be 1.

But what if csr_wr is NOT 1 for the SET? Let me check my csr_wr computation:

```systemverilog
if (csr_access_i && csr_op_en_i) begin
  unique case (csr_op_i)
    CSR_OP_READ:  csr_wr = 1'b0;
    CSR_OP_WRITE: begin csr_wdata_int = csr_wdata_i; csr_wr = 1'b1; end
    CSR_OP_SET:   begin csr_wdata_int = csr_rdata_o | csr_wdata_i; csr_wr = 1'b1; end
    CSR_OP_CLEAR: begin csr_wdata_int = csr_rdata_o & ~csr_wdata_i; csr_wr = 1'b1; end
    default: ;
  endcase
end
```

For CSR_OP_SET (value 2), csr_wr = 1. This should work.

But wait, what if the `unique case` statement is causing issues? Verilator might be optimizing the case in a way that doesn't match my expectations.

Let me also check: is the SET actually being captured by the monitor? The monitor condition is `csr_access && (csr_op_en || illegal_csr)`. If this is true, the monitor captures the transaction.

But wait, my debug output shows "op=2" for the SET. And in my case statement, CSR_OP_SET = 2. So the case should match.

Hmm, but what if there's a timing issue where the SET transaction is captured by the monitor but the write doesn't take effect because of some race condition?

Actually, wait. Let me re-read my debug output:

```
MINSTRET WRITE: wdata=e8a5dac0 rdata_before=00000000 op=2
MINSTRET WRITE: wdata=5f2399cc rdata_before=00000000 op=1
MINSTRET WRITE: wdata=1bb28a95 rdata_before=5f2399cc op=1
MINSTRET WRITE: wdata=00000000 rdata_before=1bb28a95 op=3

```

The first SET (op=2) has rdata_before=0. After the SET, minstret should be 0xe8a5dac0.
The second WRITE (op=1) has rdata_before=0. This means the SET didn't take effect!

But the second WRITE takes effect (rdata_before at step 3 is 0x5f2399cc, which is the wdata from step 2).

So WRITES work, but SETs don't! Why?

For a SET, csr_wdata_int = csr_rdata_o | csr_wdata_i. But what if csr_rdata_o is not computed correctly at the time of the SET?

Wait, but I print `rdata_before=minstret_lo_q`, which is the register value BEFORE the write. And the print is inside the always_ff block, so it's the current value of the register.

Hmm, but the rdata_before=0 for the SET. This means the register was 0 before the SET. After the SET, it should be 0 | 0xe8a5dac0 = 0xe8a5dac0. But the next transaction shows rdata_before=0, meaning the SET didn't update the register.

Wait, maybe the SET does update the register, but then something else resets it back to 0 before the next transaction.

What could reset minstret_lo_q to 0? Only:
1. rst_ni going low (reset)
2. A write with value 0
3. The counter increment (but instr_ret_i = 0)

Could there be a spurious write to MINSTRET with value 0 between the SET and the next WRITE? Let me check.

Looking at the write condition: `csr_wr && csr_addr_i == CSR_MINSTRET`. If csr_wr is true and csr_addr_i is CSR_MINSTRET, a write happens. If csr_wr is false, no write happens (and the counter stays the same since instr_ret_i = 0).

But what if csr_wr is true but csr_addr_i is NOT CSR_MINSTRET? Then no write happens to MINSTRET, and the counter stays the same. This is correct.

So the register should only change when csr_wr && csr_addr_i == CSR_MINSTRET. And my debug output shows all 5 MINSTRET writes. Between them, the register should stay the same.

But the debug shows:
- Step 1: SET, rdata_before=0, wdata=0xe8a5dac0 → after: minstret=0xe8a5dac0
- Step 2: WRITE, rdata_before=0, wdata=0x5f2399cc → after: minstret=0x5f2399cc

This is a contradiction! After step 1, minstret should be 0xe8a5dac0. But at step 2, rdata_before=0. This means minstret was reset to 0 between steps 1 and 2.

The only way this could happen is:
1. A reset occurred
2. Another write with value 0 occurred
3. The mcycle increment logic is interfering

Wait, could there be an issue with the mcycle always_ff block interfering with the minstret always_ff block?

No, they're separate always_ff blocks with separate signals. They can't interfere.

Let me add more debug output to see what's happening between the SET and WRITE transactions.

Actually, let me add debug output on EVERY clock cycle, not just when MINSTRET is written. Let me print the value of minstret_lo_q and the control signals on every cycle.

Actually, that would be too much output. Let me instead add a debug output that prints whenever minstret_lo_q changes.

Actually, let me take a different approach. Let me add a check in the always_ff block to see if minstret_lo_q is being overwritten to 0 by something.

Wait, I just realized something. My minstret always_ff block has an `else if` for the increment:

```systemverilog
if (csr_wr && csr_addr_i == CSR_MINSTRET)
  minstret_lo_q <= csr_wdata_int;
else if (~mcountinhibit_q[2] & instr_ret_i)
  minstret_lo_q <= minstret_lo_q + 32'd1;
```

But what if BOTH conditions are true? In my code, the `if` takes priority, so the write takes effect and the increment is suppressed. But what if the increment is somehow still happening?

Wait, no. The `else if` means the increment only happens when the first condition is false. So they can't both happen.

But wait, what if instr_ret_i is high (1) on some cycles? In the testbench, instr_ret_i is an unconnected input. Verilator should tie it to 0. But what if it's not?

Actually, in the ibex_cs_registers module, instr_ret_i is a regular input port. In the testbench, it's not connected. In Verilator, unconnected input ports are set to 0 (for logic type). But let me verify this.

Wait, maybe the issue is different. Let me check: is there a write to a DIFFERENT register that also writes to minstret_lo_q?

Looking at my code, minstret_lo_q is only written in one always_ff block. And it's only written when `csr_wr && csr_addr_i == CSR_MINSTRET`. So there shouldn't be any interference.

But wait, maybe there's a subtle Verilator issue. Let me check if the always_ff block is being synthesized correctly by Verilator.

Actually, let me try something. Let me print the value of minstret_lo_q on every cycle, regardless of whether a write is happening.

steps.message:
## Goal
- Restore all stripped RTL implementation files for the Ibex RISC-V core so that 5 test targets pass (tb_cs_registers, hello_test, dit_test, dummy_instr_test, pmp_smoke_test), earning proportional credit per passing test.

## Constraints & Preferences
- Cannot modify kept files: `.core` files, `dv/cs_registers/` testbench, `examples/simple_system/ibex_simple_system.cc/.h`, `examples/sw/simple_system/` (except `simple_system_common.c`), `vendor/`, `shared/`, `util/`, `lint/`, `doc/`
- Must implement ~33 empty RTL files + `ibex_simple_system.sv` + `simple_system_common.c`
- `ibex_pkg.sv` must compile first (defines all enumerations/types)
- Verilator 4.210, FuseSoC 2.4.3, riscv32-unknown-elf-gcc at `/tools/riscv/bin/`
- `ibex_core.sv` (85KB) is intact and defines all module interfaces/ports
- Default config is `small` (RV32MFast, RV32BNone, RegFileFF, no ICache, no WritebackStage, no SecureIbex, no PMPEnable)

## Progress
### Done
- Explored full codebase structure: `.core` files, testbench C++ model, SW tests, ibex_core.sv interfaces
- Implemented `rtl/ibex_pkg.sv` — enums (rv32m_e, rv32b_e, rv32zc_e, regfile_e, alu_op_e, md_op_e, pc_sel_e, exc_pc_sel_e, csr_op_e, dbg_cause_e, pmp_req_e), structs (exc_cause_t, pmp_cfg_t, pmp_mseccfg_t, irqs_t, crash_dump_t), CSR address enum (csr_num_e), constants (PMP_MAX_REGIONS, PMP_ADDR_MSB, PmpCfgRst, PmpAddrRst, PmpMseccfgRst, CSR_MIE masks, CSR_MISA_MXL, BUS_SIZE, IC params, LFSR defaults)
- Implemented `rtl/ibex_csr.sv` — simple CSR primitive with read/write, no shadow
- Implemented `rtl/ibex_counter.sv` — 64-bit counter with increment and high-word write

steps.reasoning_content:
Now I can see the issue clearly! Looking at the MSECCFG WRITE logs:

```
MSECCFG WRITE: wdata_int=97066a18 rlb=0 mmwp=0 mml=1 locks=0000
```

This sets MML=1 (because csr_wdata_int[2] = 1 and mseccfg_q.mml | 1 = 1).

Then:
```
MSECCFG WRITE: wdata_int=7adb7d8d rlb=0 mmwp=0 mml=1 locks=0000
```

This is the failing transaction (CSR Set on MSECCFG with wdata=7adb7d8d). At this point, mseccfg_q.mml is already 1 (from the previous write). So `csr_rdata_o = {29'b0, 1, 0, 0} = 4`.

But the C++ model expects `csr_rdata = 0`. This means in the C++ model, MML is still 0 at this point.

So the issue is that the WRITE that set MML=1 (wdata_int=97066a18) worked in our Verilog but NOT in the C++ model.

Wait, but why would the C++ model not set MML? Let me check:

In the C++ model, for a WRITE to MSECCFG:
```
register_value_ &= lock_mask;
register_value_ |= (newval & ~lock_mask);
```

lock_mask = 0xFFFFFFF8 (bits 2:0 unlocked, initially)
newval = csr_wdata (from the driver)

Wait, but the monitor captures `csr_rdata` from Verilog and passes it as `trans->csr_rdata`. The C++ model uses `trans->csr_wdata` as the write data. And `trans->csr_wdata = csr_wdata_i` (from the DPI monitor).

But wait, in our Verilog, for a SET operation:
- `csr_wdata_int = csr_rdata_o | csr_wdata_i`
- `csr_wr = 1`

The C++ model processes the SET operation separately: `RegisterSet(trans->csr_wdata)` where `trans->csr_wdata = csr_wdata_i` (the original wdata from the driver, NOT csr_wdata_int).

So the C++ model uses `csr_wdata_i` for SET, while our Verilog uses `csr_wdata_int` (which is `csr_rdata_o | csr_wdata_i`).

But for a WRITE operation:
- Our Verilog: `csr_wdata_int = csr_wdata_i`
- C++ model: `RegisterWrite(trans->csr_wdata)` where `trans->csr_wdata = csr_wdata_i`

These should be the same! Both use `csr_wdata_i`.

Wait, let me look at the debug output again:
```
MSECCFG WRITE: wdata_int=97066a18 rlb=0 mmwp=0 mml=1 locks=0000
```

This is a WRITE (since it's printing from the always_ff block which triggers on `csr_wr && PMPEnable && csr_addr_i == CSR_MSECCFG`). The `csr_wdata_int = 0x97066a18`, and bit 2 = 1 (MML bit). So MML gets set to 1.

But the C++ model says MML is 0 at the time of the next SET. So this WRITE must have been processed differently by the C++ model.

Wait, could this be a SET operation rather than a WRITE? Looking at the debug output, the `wdata_int=97066a18` is printed. But I can't tell from this output whether it's a WRITE or SET.

Actually, I should also print the operation type. Let me add that.

But wait, there's another possibility. What if the C++ model's MSECCFG register has a different lock_mask that prevents the MML write?

In the C++ model, GetLockMask starts with 0xFFFFFFF8 (bits 2:0 unlocked). So a WRITE with wdata[2]=1 should set MML. Unless something else affects the lock_mask.

But GetLockMask only checks:
1. If any PMP config is locked AND RLB is 0 → lock RLB
2. If MMWP is set → lock MMWP
3. If MML is set → lock MML

Initially, none of these conditions are true, so lock_mask = 0xFFFFFFF8. Bits 2:0 are fully writable.

Hmm, but what if there's a previous operation that set some other bits of MSECCFG in the C++ model but not in our Verilog?

Wait, I just realized something. The C++ model processes ALL transactions captured by the monitor. The monitor captures transactions when `csr_access && (csr_op_en || illegal_csr)`. If `illegal_csr` is 0, the monitor captures the transaction.

But what if there's a transaction where `illegal_csr` is 1 in the C++ model but 0 in our Verilog? This would cause the C++ model to not process the transaction, while our Verilog processes it.

Actually wait, the `illegal_csr` signal comes from our Verilog, not the C++ model. The C++ model's ProcessTransaction doesn't check `illegal_csr`. It just matches the address and processes the operation.

But the C++ model does check `matched` in NewTransaction. If no register matches the address, `matched = false`, and the model checks if `illegal_csr` is set. If `illegal_csr` is 0 but no register matches, the test fails.

This is different from our Verilog's `illegal_csr` signal. Our Verilog sets `illegal_csr = 1` for certain addresses. The C++ model also considers these addresses as non-existent (NonImpRegister).

Wait, but the C++ model creates NonImpRegister for some addresses. NonImpRegister DOES match the address (MatchAddr returns true). So `matched = true`, and the model processes the transaction. NonImpRegister returns 0 for all operations.

So the C++ model DOES process transactions for NonImpRegister addresses. And it compares the read value (0) with the captured `csr_rdata` from Verilog.

OK, I think the issue might be that the C++ model has a NonImpRegister at the MSECCFG address (0x747) when PMPEnable is 0, but a MSeccfgRegister when PMPEnable is 1.

Looking at the C++ model:
```cpp
register_map_.push_back(
    std::make_unique<MSeccfgRegister>(kCSRMSeccfg, &register_map_));
register_map_.push_back(
    std::make_unique<NonImpRegister>(kCSRMSeccfgh, &register_map_));
```

MSECCFG is ALWAYS created as MSeccfgRegister, regardless of PMPEnable! And MSECCFGH is always NonImpRegister.

So in the C++ model, MSECCFG always exists and is always a MSeccfgRegister. In our Verilog, MSECCFG is accessible when PMPEnable is 1 (otherwise `illegal_csr = 1`).

But since PMPEnable is 1 in this test, both models have MSECCFG accessible. So the `illegal_csr` issue doesn't apply here.

Let me look at this from yet another angle. The C++ model's MSeccfgRegister always exists. But its GetLockMask depends on the PMP config lock state. Specifically:

```cpp
if (AnyPmpCfgsLocked() && ((register_value_ & kMSeccfgRlb) == 0)) {
    lock_mask |= kMSeccfgRlb;
}
```

`AnyPmpCfgsLocked()` checks if any PmpCfgRegister has a lock bit set. But if PMPEnable is 0, the C++ model creates NonImpRegister for PMPCfg0-3, not PmpCfgRegister. So `AnyPmpCfgsLocked()` would check PmpCfgRegister entries, but there are none when PMPEnable is 0.

Wait, but PMPEnable is 1 in this test. So there ARE PmpCfgRegister entries.

OK, I think I need to check the C++ model's AnyPmpCfgsLocked more carefully. It iterates through the register map looking for registers that match `kCSRPMPCfg0` with a mask of `0xfffffffc`. This matches PMPCfg0, PMPCfg1, PMPCfg2, PMPCfg3 (all have addresses 0x3A0-0x3A3).

When PMPEnable is 1 and PMPNumRegions = 4:
- PMPCfg0 (0x3A0) is a PmpCfgRegister (regions 0-3, 4 regions / 4 = 1 CFG register)
- PMPCfg1-3 (0x3A1-0x3A3) are NonImpRegister

So `AnyPmpCfgsLocked()` checks PMPCfg0's value for lock bits.

Wait, but what about the `for (unsigned int i = 0; i < 4; i++)` loop in the C++ model?
```cpp
for (unsigned int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
    uint32_t reg_addr = 0x3A0 + i;
    if (params->PMPEnable && (i < (params->PMPNumRegions / 4))) {
      register_map_.push_back(
          std::make_unique<PmpCfgRegister>(reg_addr, &register_map_));
    } else {
      register_map_.push_back(
          std::make_unique<NonImpRegister>(reg_addr, &register_map_));
    }
}
```

With PMPEnable=1 and PMPNumRegions=4:
- i=0: 0 < (4/4) = 0 < 1 → PmpCfgRegister at 0x3A0 ✓
- i=1: 1 < 1 → false → NonImpRegister at 0x3A1
- i=2: 2 < 1 → false → NonImpRegister at 0x3A2
- i=3: 3 < 1 → false → NonImpRegister at 0x3A3

So only PMPCfg0 (0x3A0) is a PmpCfgRegister. PMPCfg1-3 are NonImpRegister.

Now, `AnyPmpCfgsLocked()` checks:
```cpp
for (auto &reg : *map_pointer_) {
    if (reg->MatchAddr(kCSRPMPCfg0, 0xfffffffc)) {
      if ((reg->RegisterRead() & 0x80808080) != 0) {
        return true;
      }
    }
}
```

This checks all registers that match `kCSRPMPCfg0 & 0xfffffffc = 0x3A0`. The mask `0xfffffffc` means the bottom 2 bits are ignored. So addresses 0x3A0, 0x3A1, 0x3A2, 0x3A3 all match.

But wait, `MatchAddr` with mask `0xfffffffc`:
```cpp
bool BaseRegister::MatchAddr(uint32_t addr, uint32_t addr_mask) {
  return ((addr & addr_mask) == (register_address_ & addr_mask));
}
```

So `MatchAddr(0x3A0, 0xfffffffc)` checks if `(0x3A0 & 0xfffffffc) == (reg_addr & 0xfffffffc)`.

For PMPCfg0 (0x3A0): `0x3A0 & 0xfffffffc = 0x3A0 == 0x3A0 & 0xfffffffc = 0x3A0` → match
For PMPCfg1 (0x3A1): `0x3A0 & 0xfffffffc = 0x3A0 == 0x3A1 & 0xfffffffc = 0x3A0` → match!
For PMPCfg2 (0x3A2): `0x3A0 == 0x3A0` → match!
For PMPCfg3 (0x3A3): `0x3A0 == 0x3A0` → match!

So `AnyPmpCfgsLocked()` checks the value of ALL four PMPCfg registers (0x3A0-0x3A3). Since PMPCfg1-3 are NonImpRegister (always return 0), their lock bits are never set. So `AnyPmpCfgsLocked()` only returns true if PMPCfg0 (0x3A0) has a lock bit set.

This should be the same in our Verilog. When any of pmp_cfg_q[0-3] has lock=1, we consider PMP configs as locked.

But wait, in our Verilog MSECCFG write logic, we check:
```
if (!mseccfg_q.rlb && !(|{pmp_cfg_q[0].lock, pmp_cfg_q[1].lock,

    mseccfg_q.rlb <= csr_wdata_int[0];
else if (!mseccfg_q.rlb)

```

Wait, this is for the RLB write condition. The C++ model locks RLB when any PMP config is locked AND RLB is 0. In our Verilog, we allow writing RLB when `!rlb && !any_locked`. If `!rlb && any_locked`, we set `rlb <= 0` (keeping it 0).

But for MML, we still use:
```
mseccfg_q.mml <= csr_wdata_int[2] | mseccfg_q.mml;
```

This doesn't depend on the PMP lock state. And the C++ model also doesn't lock MML based on PMP locks. So MML should be set the same way in both models.

OK, I think the issue might be that the C++ model doesn't set MML in a previous transaction, while our Verilog does. Let me trace through the specific transaction.

The debug shows:
```
MSECCFG WRITE: wdata_int=97066a18 rlb=0 mmwp=0 mml=1 locks=0000
```

This is a WRITE (not SET or CLEAR, since it's triggered by `csr_wr`). The `wdata_int = 0x97066a18`. Let me check bit 2: 0x18 = 0b00011000, bit 2 = 0. Wait, the whole value is 0x97066a18:
- 0x97066a18 in binary: 1001_0111_0000_0110_0110_1010_0001_1000
- Bit 2: 0 (bit 2 of 0x18 = 0b00011000, bit 2 is 0)

Wait, that can't be right. The debug says `mml=1` after this write, but `csr_wdata_int[2] = 0`? Let me re-check.

0x97066a18:
- Hex: 9 7 0 6 6 a 1 8
- Binary: 1001 0111 0000 0110 0110 1010 0001 1000
- Bit 0: 0
- Bit 1: 0
- Bit 2: 0
- Bit 3: 1
- Bit 4: 1

So bit 2 is 0! But the debug says `mml=1`. And the write logic is:
```
mseccfg_q.mml <= csr_wdata_int[2] | mseccfg_q.mml;
```

If `csr_wdata_int[2] = 0` and `mseccfg_q.mml = 0`, then `mml <= 0 | 0 = 0`. But the debug shows `mml=1`.

This means `mseccfg_q.mml` was ALREADY 1 before this write! But the debug also shows `mml=1` for this entry. Wait, the debug prints the current value of mseccfg_q, which is the value BEFORE the write (since the always_ff block hasn't updated yet).

No wait, in Verilog, the always_ff block uses non-blocking assignments. So `mseccfg_q.mml` at the time of the `$display` is the OLD value. The `$display` shows `mml=1`, which is the OLD value before the write.

So the question is: when did MML become 1?

Let me look at the previous MSECCFG WRITE:
```
MSECCFG WRITE: wdata_int=a23a953f rlb=0 mmwp=1 mml=1 locks=0000
```

This shows `mml=1` before this write. And `wdata_int=0xa23a953f`, bit 2 = 1 (0x3f = 0011_1111, bit 2 = 1). So this write sets MML. Wait, but the debug shows `mml=1` as the OLD value, and `wdata_int[2] = 1`. So `mml <= 1 | 1 = 1` (MML was already 1, and stays 1).


Wait, I think there might be a deeper issue. The C++ model's lock mask approach is fundamentally different from my Verilog approach. In the C++ model:

For WRITE: `register_value_ = (register_value_ & lock_mask) | (newval & ~lock_mask)`
For SET: `register_value_ = register_value_ | (newval & ~lock_mask)`
For CLEAR: `register_value_ = register_value_ & (~newval | lock_mask)`

The key insight is that `csr_wdata_int` in my Verilog already incorporates the operation (SET = OR, CLEAR = AND-NOT, WRITE = replace). And then I apply the lock conditions.

For SET: `csr_wdata_int = csr_rdata_o | csr_wdata_i`
The C++ model computes: `register_value_ | (newval & ~lock_mask)`

For unlocked bits: `csr_wdata_int = csr_rdata_o | csr_wdata_i` matches `register_value_ | newval`
For locked bits: `csr_wdata_int` includes the OR result, but the C++ model keeps the original value.

In my new Verilog code, for locked bits (MML=1), I don't write (`if (!mseccfg_q.mml)` is false). So the value stays. This matches the C++ model.

For unlocked bits, I write `csr_wdata_int[bit]`. For SET, `csr_wdata_int = csr_rdata_o | csr_wdata_i`. So `csr_wdata_int[bit] = register_value_[bit] | csr_wdata_i[bit]`. This matches the C++ model's `register_value_[bit] | newval[bit]`.

For WRITE: `csr_wdata_int = csr_wdata_i`. For unlocked bits, I write `csr_wdata_i[bit]`. This matches the C++ model's `(newval & ~lock_mask)[bit] = newval[bit]`.

For CLEAR: `csr_wdata_int = csr_rdata_o & ~csr_wdata_i`. For unlocked bits, I write `(csr_rdata_o & ~csr_wdata_i)[bit]`. This matches the C++ model's `register_value_[bit] & ~newval[bit]`.

OK so the logic should be correct with my new code. Let me build and test.

But wait, I'm still confused about why MMWP went from 1 to 0 in my previous debug output. With the old code:
```
mseccfg_q.mmwp <= csr_wdata_int[1] | mseccfg_q.mmwp;
```

This can NEVER clear MMWP once it's set. So how did MMWP become 0?

The only explanation is a reset. But MML stayed at 1, which contradicts a reset.

Unless... the debug output is not showing all MSECCFG writes. Maybe there are MSECCFG writes that happen during reset cycles that aren't being printed (because the reset branch takes priority).

Let me check: in the always_ff block:
```
if (!rst_ni) begin
    mseccfg_q <= PMPRstMsecCfg;
end else if (csr_wr && ...) begin
    ...
    $display(...);
end
```

During a reset cycle, the first branch is taken, and the $display is not executed. So I wouldn't see the reset.

But after the reset, the next MSECCFG write would show the reset values. And if there's a MSECCFG write that sets MML but not MMWP, the debug would show `mmwp=0, mml=1` BEFORE the write (because MML was already set by a previous write after the reset).

Wait, but the debug shows `mml=1` BEFORE the write. If there was a reset, `mml` would be 0. So there must have been a MSECCFG write between the reset and this one that set MML=1. And that intermediate write would be shown in the debug output.

1. There's a missing debug entry (but I print every MSECCFG write)
2. MMWP was cleared by something other than a MSECCFG write (impossible with the OR logic)
3. The MMWP value in the debug is wrong

Hmm, actually, could there be an issue with the $display timing? In Verilator, $display in always_ff blocks is executed at the simulation time of the clock edge. But the NBA assignment `mseccfg_q.mmwp <= ...` takes effect after the always_ff block.

So at the time of the $display, `mseccfg_q.mmwp` shows the value from the PREVIOUS cycle. The new value (from the current cycle's write) will take effect after the NBA.

But the debug shows the old value. So if the previous write set MMWP=1, and then the current write's debug shows `mmwp=0`, it means the previous write didn't actually set MMWP=1.

Wait, that doesn't make sense. Let me re-read the debug output:

```
MSECCFG WRITE: wdata_int=a23a953f rlb=0 mmwp=1 mml=1 locks=0000
```

This shows `mmwp=1` BEFORE this write. So MMWP was already 1. And this write might or might not change it.

```
MSECCFG WRITE: wdata_int=97066a18 rlb=0 mmwp=0 mml=1 locks=0000
```

This shows `mmwp=0` BEFORE this write. So MMWP was cleared between the two writes.

With the OR logic, MMWP can't be cleared by a MSECCFG write. So the only way is a reset.

But MML is 1 in both entries. If there was a reset, MML would also be 0. So there must have been a MSECCFG write AFTER the reset that set MML=1.

But that write should appear in the debug output. Unless... the write happened during a reset cycle?

Wait, during a reset cycle, the `if (!rst_ni)` branch is taken, which resets the register. But `csr_wr` might still be set if the driver is driving a transaction. However, the reset branch has priority, so the MSECCFG write doesn't happen.

But what if `rst_ni` goes high DURING the same cycle? In Verilator, this shouldn't happen because `rst_ni` is updated by the DPI function at the clock edge.

OK, I think the issue might be that there are MSECCFG writes that happen during cycles where `rst_ni` is transitioning. Let me not worry about this and just rebuild with the new logic.

Actually, I just realized something else. Maybe the issue is that the C++ model resets MSECCFG when it sees `!rst_n` in the monitor, but the timing might be different from our Verilog's async reset.

In the C++ model:
```cpp
if (!rst_n) {
    reg_model_->RegisterReset();
}
```

This is called in `CaptureTransaction`, which is called by `monitor_tick`. And `rst_n` is the Verilog signal `rst_ni`.

In our Verilog:
```
always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
    if (!rst_ni) begin
        mseccfg_q <= PMPRstMsecCfg;
    end
```

The async reset triggers on `negedge rst_ni`. But in Verilator (cycle-accurate), this is evaluated at the clock edge.

The key question is: when `rst_ni` goes low, does the C++ model reset at the same time as our Verilog?

In the testbench:
```
assign rst_ni = in_rst_ni & dpi_rst_ni;

always_ff @(posedge clk_i) begin
    env_dpi::env_tick(stop_simulation, test_passed);
    rst_dpi::rst_tick("rstn_driver", dpi_rst_ni);
end

always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni) begin
    reg_dpi::monitor_tick("reg_driver",
                          rst_ni,
                          ...);
end
```

On a clock edge where `dpi_rst_ni` goes low:
1. `rst_dpi::rst_tick` sets `dpi_rst_ni = 0`
2. `rst_ni = in_rst_ni & dpi_rst_ni = 1 & 0 = 0`
3. In the second always_ff, the `negedge rst_ni` triggers the async reset in our cs_registers module
4. `monitor_tick` captures the transaction with `rst_n = 0`
5. C++ model resets

So the reset happens at the same time in both models. ✓

But wait, there might be a race condition. In the first always_ff, `dpi_rst_ni` is set to 0. But in the second always_ff, `rst_ni` is already 0 (because it's a combinational signal). However, in Verilator, the order of always_ff block evaluation is not guaranteed.

Actually, in Verilator, all always_ff blocks at the same edge are evaluated in a deterministic order based on the dependency graph. But the DPI calls are not part of the dependency graph - they're external.

Hmm, this is getting really complicated. Let me just rebuild and see if the new MSECCFG logic fixes the test.

Wait, actually, I think there might be a much simpler issue. Let me re-examine the MSECCFG write logic I just wrote:

```
if (!(any_pmp_cfg_locked && !mseccfg_q.rlb))
    mseccfg_q.rlb <= csr_wdata_int[0];
if (!mseccfg_q.mmwp)

if (!mseccfg_q.mml)

```

For a WRITE operation: `csr_wdata_int = csr_wdata_i`

If `mseccfg_q.mml = 0` and `csr_wdata_i[2] = 0`:
- `if (!mseccfg_q.mml)` is true → `mseccfg_q.mml <= 0` (stays 0) ✓

If `mseccfg_q.mml = 0` and `csr_wdata_i[2] = 1`:
- `if (!mseccfg_q.mml)` is true → `mseccfg_q.mml <= 1` ✓

If `mseccfg_q.mml = 1`:
- `if (!mseccfg_q.mml)` is false → no assignment → `mseccfg_q.mml` stays 1 ✓

For a SET: `csr_wdata_int = csr_rdata_o | csr_wdata_i`

If `mseccfg_q.mml = 0` and `csr_wdata_i[2] = 1`:

- `if (!mseccfg_q.mml)` is true → `mseccfg_q.mml <= 1` ✓

If `mseccfg_q.mml = 1`:
- `if (!mseccfg_q.mml)` is false → no assignment → `mseccfg_q.mml` stays 1 ✓

For a CLEAR: `csr_wdata_int = csr_rdata_o & ~csr_wdata_i`

If `mseccfg_q.mml = 0`:
- `csr_wdata_int[2] = 0 & ~csr_wdata_i[2] = 0`
- `if (!mseccfg_q.mml)` is true → `mseccfg_q.mml <= 0` (stays 0) ✓

If `mseccfg_q.mml = 1`:
- `csr_wdata_int[2] = 1 & ~csr_wdata_i[2]`
  - If `csr_wdata_i[2] = 0`: `csr_wdata_int[2] = 1`
  - If `csr_wdata_i[2] = 1`: `csr_wdata_int[2] = 0`
- `if (!mseccfg_q.mml)` is false → no assignment → `mseccfg_q.mml` stays 1 ✓

- kMSeccfgMmwp = 0x2 (bit 1)
